detail.longDescription: (Apologies for the childish self-censoring, but A) I'm serious about it and B) it kinda drives home my point on its own...) More specifically: why continue the practice of pushing content off the front page that has a healthy discussion, and preventing content that gets multiple comments early on from reaching it in the first place? I've been tilting at the windmill of Markdown support on this site for years now, through which I've learned that all three mods are undeniably well-meaning, competent people. Even when seemingly suspicious actions are taken --like downranking any post that mentioned the NSA in the wake of Snowden-- I feel confident that the actions are taken in good faith. Namely, they seem to prioritize: 1. Prevention of 'flame wars', which imply vitriol but also a tit-for-tat between two 'sides'. This is why you can't downvote replies to your comment, you get tempbanned for a few hours if posting comments that get downvoted, etc.; there's lots of mechanisms in play. 2. Prevention of spam. Doesn't relate to this issue. 3. Maintenance of a respectful, ~professional culture. This is the big one here, I think. By killing discussions about politics, white vs. blue dresses, Rust rewrites, and other issues people are more passionate about than they are about local-first CRDTs and the rise of WASM, the culture is made professional on a substrate level. I just don't think that's enough to justify this feature, though. There's a lot to say in response, but to keep it as short as possible: A) This is prioritizing a vision of HackerNews as a newsletter for startup founders rather than a community at the heart of (anglophone?) tech, which is obviously becoming more important by the day. We're already well past the point where LLM-based tools can produce a far better, more personalized, fairer, and more diverse newsletter than a forum could hope to, anyway. B) It's taking a shortcut when there's no need for one, if they accepted help in the form of volunteer moderators below the admins (they're ubiquitous elsewhere for a reason) and/or sponsorship from tech firms to fund staff, possibly in exchange for a subtle shoutout in the footer. C) As Reddit spirals into a steep dive[1] and LessWrong spirals upwards in an ever-tighter (light)cone[2], this is the only sizeable forum left of any quality for discussing science and technology. As AI gets better forums are losing their utility as a place to crowdsource objective answers, sure, but I'd argue they're more important than ever for understanding the trickier issues that are coming to define our society. TL;DR: I can't help but shake the impression that HN is fleeing from the future and its founders' (I count the admins, dang-it!) stated ideals regarding freedom, democracy, and epistemic agency. Not the future, actually: the present . [1]: https://www.businessinsider.com/reddit-ad-growth-plans-search-shopping-ai-agents-2026-11 [2]: https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/kmruNMEMK5uN3LH6n/notes-on-the-decline-of-lesswrong-s-great-writers --- To be clear, I am serious about the "Ask" part of this "Ask HN", despite giving an argument; this truly baffles me. What do you y'all think? What am I missing?
